# Scleritis and episcleritis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Conjunctive, sclera, and cornea > Scleritis and episcleritis*

[Original Article Link](/library/KO0UtT)

---

## Summary

<u>Scleritis</u> is an inflammatory condition that affects the <u>sclera</u>, while <u>episcleritis</u> is an inflammatory condition that affects the <u>episclera</u>. Because the <u>episclera</u> is the outermost layer of the <u>sclera</u>, <u>episcleritis</u> is a more <u>superficial</u> condition. While the etiology of <u>episcleritis</u> is usually <u>idiopathic</u>, <u>scleritis</u> often occurs in individuals with underlying systemic disease (e.g., <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u>). Both conditions can also be caused by infections or reactions to medications. They are diagnosed based on the <u>patient history</u> and <u>physical examination</u>. A search for underlying systemic illness is especially important when <u>scleritis</u> is diagnosed, but it is also warranted in suspected <u>episcleritis</u> if there are other signs of systemic disease present (e.g., <u>arthritis</u>, <u>rash</u>). Systemic treatment with <u>corticosteroids</u> is generally required in necrotizing <u>scleritis</u>, <u>scleritis</u> that does not resolve with <u>NSAIDs</u>, and <u>scleritis</u> affecting the <u>posterior</u> portion of the <u>sclera</u>. In refractory cases, <u>immunosuppressive drugs</u> may be required. <u>Episcleritis</u> typically regresses after 1–2 weeks, and treatment is not necessary in most cases.

---

## Episcleritis

* Definition: inflammation of the <u>episclera</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[1]](/library/wyYhh7)[[2]](/library/9yYNh7)

* Mean age: ∼ 45 years

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Unilateral in up to 70% of cases

* Etiology [[3]](/library/CyYqh7)

* Most commonly <u>idiopathic</u>

* Associated with underlying systemic disease in a minority of cases  (most commonly <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>)

* Less common causes

* Bacterial/viral infection

* Drug reaction (e.g., <u>bisphosphonates</u>)

* Clinical features

* Acute onset of symptoms

* Mild <u>eye pain</u>/irritation and watering

* <u>Eye</u> redness

* <u>Vision</u> is not affected

* Subtypes and variants

* Simple/diffuse <u>episcleritis</u>: most common subtype

* Nodular/focal <u>episcleritis</u>: prolonged inflammation, usually occurring in patients with underlying systemic disease

* Diagnostics

* Diagnosed based on <u>patient history</u> and <u>physical examination</u>

* Vasoconstricting <u>eye</u> drops (<u>phenylephrine</u>) may allow <u>episcleritis</u> to be differentiated from <u>scleritis</u>. [[4]](/library/xyYEh7)

* Further diagnostics are required if systemic disease is suspected.

* Treatment

* Symptomatic treatment (e.g., cold compresses, <u>eye</u> lubrication)

* In persistent or severe cases: <u>NSAIDs</u> and/or <u>topical steroids</u>

* Treatment of any underlying conditions

* Prognosis [[1]](/library/wyYhh7)[[5]](/library/ByYzh7)

* In most cases, spontaneous regression occurs after 1–2 weeks.

* Recurrent bouts of the disease may occur every 1–3 months.

* Rarely progresses to reduced <u>visual acuity</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Although <u>episcleritis</u> is usually <u>self-limiting</u>, it manifests similarly to other, less innocuous conditions of the <u>eye</u> (e.g., <u>scleritis</u>, <u>keratitis</u>) that do require treatment. These conditions should be ruled out prior to diagnosing <u>episcleritis</u> (see “Differential diagnoses” below).

---

## Scleritis

* Definition: <u>transmural</u> inflammation of the <u>sclera</u>

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[6]](/library/yyYd37)

* Mean age: 40–60 years

* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Bilateral in up to 50% of cases

* Etiology

* In up to 60% of patients, <u>scleritis</u> is associated with an underlying systemic disorder or infection (most commonly <u>rheumatoid arthritis</u>, but also <u>SLE</u>, <u>granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>, <u>polymyositis</u>, and <u>gout</u>).

* May also be <u>idiopathic</u>

* Subtypes and variants

* <u>Anterior</u> <u>scleritis</u>

* Non-necrotizing (nodular or diffuse)

* Necrotizing

* With inflammation (severe <u>pain</u> and <u>eye</u> redness)

* Without inflammation (painless) → scleromalacia perforans

* <u>Posterior</u> <u>scleritis</u>

* Clinical features [[7]](/library/AyYR37)[[8]](/library/_yY537)

* Subacute onset of symptoms

* Severe deep, aching, and boring <u>eye pain</u> that is exacerbated by <u>eye</u> movement;   and palpation; may radiate to the rest of the face

* <u>Eye</u> redness

* <u>Photophobia</u> and/or loss of <u>vision</u>

* Fixed scleral <u>nodules</u> (esp. in <u>anterior</u> nodular <u>scleritis</u>)

* Scleral thinning (esp. in <u>scleromalacia perforans</u>): may appear as violet or blue discoloration of the <u>eye</u>

* Diagnostics [[9]](/library/zyYr37)

* Diagnosis based on history and <u>physical examination</u>

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: to detect signs of <u>posterior</u> <u>scleritis</u>

* Orbital CT/<u>MRI</u>: to differentiate between orbital lesions, e.g., tumors, and <u>posterior</u> <u>scleritis</u> [[9]](/library/zyYr37)

* Workup for potential systemic disease (e.g., RF, <u>ANA</u>, <u>ANCA</u>, and <u>HLA</u> typing)

* Treatment [[10]](/library/-yYD37)

* <u>NSAIDs</u>: first-line therapy in mild to moderate cases

* <u>Systemic glucocorticoids</u>: in <u>posterior</u> or necrotizing <u>scleritis</u>; patients unresponsive to <u>NSAIDs</u>

* Systemic <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u> (e.g., <u>azathioprine</u>, <u>methotrexate</u>): in patients unresponsive to <u>steroids</u>

* Scleral <u>transplantation</u>: in patients with impending perforation

* Treatment of any underlying systemic conditions

* Prognosis: Recurrent bouts of disease often occur if <u>scleritis</u> is not treated → <u>cataracts</u>, corneal changes, <u>glaucoma</u>, and even permanent loss of <u>vision</u> [[11]](/library/ZAYZR7)

> [!NOTE]
> In a patient with focal <u>eye pain</u> with tenderness to palpation of the <u>eye</u>, with or without violet discoloration of the <u>sclera</u>, an ophthalmologic consult is warranted!




> [!NOTE]
> In order to diagnose <u>scleritis</u>, a workup should be done to evaluate for underlying systemic disease!

## Differential diagnoses

|  | <u>Scleritis</u> | <u>Episcleritis</u> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Most common etiology | <br>* Systemic inflammation or infection<br><br> | <br>* <u>Idiopathic</u><br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* Subacute onset<br><br>* Severe <u>pain</u> exacerbated by <u>eye</u> movement<br><br>* Visual disturbances and <u>photophobia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Acute onset<br><br>* Mild <u>pain</u>/irritation<br><br>* <u>Eye</u> redness, watering<br><br>* Normal <u>vision</u>, no <u>photophobia</u><br><br><br> |
| Diagnostics | <br><br>* <u>Phenylephrine</u> <u>eye</u> drops → nonblanching<br><br>* Blue coloration of the <u>eye</u> (deep inflammation)<br><br>* <u>Eye</u> changes (e.g., <u>nodules</u>, thinning of the <u>sclera</u>, corneal changes)<br><br>* Signs of systemic illness (e.g., <u>arthritis</u>, <u>rash</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Phenylephrine</u> <u>eye</u> drops → blanching<br><br>* <u>Eye</u> redness (<u>superficial</u> inflammation)<br><br><br> |
| Treatment | <br><br>* Systemic <u>steroids</u><br><br>* <u>NSAIDs</u><br><br>* <u>Antibiotics</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Typically <u>self-limiting</u><br><br>* <u>Topical steroids</u> if refractory<br><br><br> |
| Prognosis | <br>* Permanent partial loss of <u>vision</u> is possible.<br><br> | <br>* Rarely progresses to reduced <u>visual acuity</u><br><br> |




* Other diagnoses to consider

* <u>Conjunctivitis</u>

* Herpes <u>keratitis</u>

* <u>Uveitis</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.
